builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class: A Policed Quality-of-Service Mechanism for Agentic AI Traffic, Evaluated from Simulation to Real-Kernel Adversarial Testing
summary: The method replaces trusted DiffServ marking and per-flow fair queuing (fq_codel) with a reserved DSCP value for agent traffic plus a router-side classifier that demotes flows contradicting their declared class, backed by a rate-limited priority queue. The cost is router configuration and classifier deployment on network equipment, plus up to a 12% increase in human-traffic delay and the risk of demoting legitimate flows when the classifier errs. It can fail in practice because most gains came from the separate class rather than verification, a four-feature live classifier missed six spoofers that copied the agent pattern, and the timing feature stopped separating agent from human flows under emulated network delay; all evaluation was synthetic or sandbox-scale.
rationale: This is a network-layer QoS mechanism requiring control of routers and kernel configuration, not an LLM inference or agent-engineering technique the reader can adopt on a single GPU or through APIs, and its evidence base is limited to simulation and sandbox-scale kernel tests.
technique: Verifiable DSCP traffic class for agent flows

claims.statement: The method replaces trusted DiffServ marking and per-flow fair queuing (fq_codel) with a reserved DSCP value for agent traffic plus a router-side classifier that demotes flows contradicting their declared class, backed by a rate-limited priority queue. The cost is router configuration and classifier deployment on network equipment, plus up to a 12% increase in human-traffic delay and the risk of demoting legitimate flows when the classifier errs. It can fail in practice because most gains came from the separate class rather than verification, a four-feature live classifier missed six spoofers that copied the agent pattern, and the timing feature stopped separating agent from human flows under emulated network delay; all evaluation was synthetic or sandbox-scale.

Under a spoofed flood on a real Linux kernel, VATC's rate limit held human latency 11 times below DiffServ's; in a constructed burst it cut mean agent queuing delay by 98% relative to DiffServ in simulation.
